2013.324.title: Portrait of Raja Jagat Singh of Nurpur (reigned 1618–46)
culture: Mughal India, Court of Jahangir (reigned 1605 - 27), possibly Lahore
2013.324.tech: Gum tempera and gold on paper
2013.324.dims: Painting only: 19.1 x 11.6 cm (7 1/2 x 4 9/16 in.); Page: 41 x 32.7 cm (16 1/8 x 12 7/8 in.)
2013.324.desc: Jagat Singh was a prince from a small kingdom in the western Himalayan foothills who grew up at the imperial Mughal court of Jahangir and his queen Nur Jahan. He was given the title of prince in 1619, and this painting may commemorate that event. Very few nobles from the hill states had positions at the Mughal court at this time, so his portrait is a rare imperial Mughal painting.The emperor and his favorite wife frequently visited Nurpur, named “City of Light” in their honor, to hunt and relax, and Prince Jagat Singh was a favorite of the queen. She interceded on his behalf in 1624, when he joined a rebellion to dethrone her husband.

2013.327.title: Portrait of Murad Bakhsh (1624–61)
culture: Mughal India, court of Shah Jahan (reigned 1628–58)
2013.327.tech: gum tempera and gold on paper
2013.327.desc: The miniature portrait of a Mughal prince is now mounted on an album page. Originally, it was in a gemstone setting as a “portrait jewel” to be worn by family and supporters at court. India’s ruling elite had been wearing portrait jewels since Sir Thomas Rowe (about 1581–1655) presented British portrait miniatures and cameos to the Mughal emperor as part of a diplomatic gift in 1616, when he successfully negotiated for British access to India’s ports.

1932.118.title: The heroine who waits anxiously for her absent lover (Utka Nayika)
1932.118.desc: Night has fallen. Love, moonlight, stars, and jasmine give the heroine the courage to face its dangers, but with a heightened sense of worry. Rain clouds approach, and the artist communicates her anxiety with nervous hand gestures and restless feet. She arranged a bed of leaves, but there is still no sign of her lover.Pale colors, distant cityscapes, and wooded settings became popular in Pahari paintings of the late 1700s. Her long legs and eyes, as well as the proportions of her round head distinguish most Pahari paintings of this period.

2018.168.title: Maru Ragini, from a Ragamala (Garland of Melodies)
culture: Northwestern India, Rajasthan, Rajput Kingdom of Amber or Southwestern India, Deccan
2018.168.tech: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
2018.168.desc: A Rajput warrior holding a spear, with piercing dagger (katar) and sword attached to his belt, stands alone with his camel in a landscape. They have arrived at the banks of a stream, verdant in contrast to the intense hot yellow of the ground behind them. The musical mode associated with this painting is based on folk melodies of Rajasthan, where local stories feature a hero with a camel mount.
